title: Common warehouse metamodel
text:
Specification for modeling in data warehouse

The **common warehouse metamodel** (**CWM**) defines a specification for modeling [metadata](/wiki/Metadata "Metadata") for [relational](/wiki/RDBMS "RDBMS"), non-relational, [multi-dimensional](/wiki/Multidimensional_database "Multidimensional database"), and most other objects found in a [data warehousing](/wiki/Data_warehouse "Data warehouse") environment. The specification is released and owned by the [Object Management Group](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group"), which also claims a trademark in the use of "CWM".[[1]](#cite_note-1)
breadcrumb: Category:Data warehousing products > Common warehouse metamodel

title: Common warehouse metamodel
text:
## Overview

The CWM specifies interfaces that can be used to enable interchange of warehouse and business intelligence metadata between warehouse tools, warehouse platforms and warehouse metadata repositories in distributed heterogeneous environments. CWM is based on three standards:

- [UML](/wiki/Unified_Modeling_Language "Unified Modeling Language") – Unified Modeling Language, an [OMG](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group") modeling standard
- [MOF](/wiki/Meta-Object_Facility "Meta-Object Facility") – Meta Object Facility, an [OMG](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group") metamodeling and metadata repository standard
- [XMI](/wiki/XML_Metadata_Interchange "XML Metadata Interchange") – XML Metadata Interchange, an [OMG](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group") metadata interchange standard

CWM models enable users to trace the lineage of data – CWM provides objects that describe where the data came from and when and how the data was created. Instances of the metamodel are exchanged via [XML Metadata Interchange](/wiki/XML_Metadata_Interchange "XML Metadata Interchange") (XMI) documents.

Initially, CWM contained a local definition for a data translation facility. It is not clear how the [QVT](/wiki/QVT "QVT") final adopted specification[[2]](#cite_note-2) will affect CWM.

title: Common warehouse metamodel
text:
### Compliance with the CWM specification

Software vendors claiming CWM support differ in the degree to which they comply with CWM. Some were co-submitters of the specification, and are actively using the OMG trademark in marketing literature. Other vendors have expressed support for CWM or claim they have products that are "CWM-compliant."

Questions about compliance are addressed within the specification itself. Chapter 18 in both the 1.0 and 1.1 specification list required and optional compliance points.

The Object Management Group has a list of CWM implementations, but it is unclear how this list is maintained.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

title: Common warehouse metamodel
text:
### Interoperability of CWM tools

Compliance with the CWM specification does not guarantee tools from different vendors will integrate well, even when they are "CWM-compliant". The OMG addressed some of these issues by releasing patterns and best practices to correct these problems in a supplementary specification, [CWM Metadata Interchange Patterns](/w/index.php?title=CWM_Metadata_Interchange_Patterns&action=edit&redlink=1 "CWM Metadata Interchange Patterns (page does not exist)")[[4]](#cite_note-4)

- [Oracle Corporation](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation") Oracle Warehouse Builder and [Oracle SQL Developer Data Modeler](/w/index.php?title=Oracle_SQL_Developer_Data_Modeler&action=edit&redlink=1 "Oracle SQL Developer Data Modeler (page does not exist)") (formerly known as IKAN CWM4ALL)

- [SAS](/wiki/SAS_Institute "SAS Institute") SAS adheres to the Object Management Group's CWM as the interoperability and interchange standard. An alliance between SAS and Meta Integration Technology Inc. (MITI) enables SAS to provide bridges for sharing and exchanging metadata with more than 40 design tool and repository vendors[[6]](#cite_note-6)

### Other vendors supporting CWM

The following products or companies have claimed CWM support, but are not listed by OMG as having a CWM implementation. In some cases, the vendor may have implemented the v1.0 specification, which was replaced by the v1.1 specification. Refer to the software vendor to determine if the product is compliant with CWM or merely supports a subset of the required portions of the specification.

- [Cognos](/wiki/Cognos "Cognos"), now a division of [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), is listed as a supporter of CWM in the v1.1 specification. Cognos product literature claims support for "Common Warehouse Model (CWM)" but never mentions an actual [OMG](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group") specification.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
- [Hyperion Solutions](/wiki/Hyperion_Solutions "Hyperion Solutions"), now a division of [Oracle Corporation](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation")
- InQuisient fully supports version 1.1 in its data repository.
- [Pentaho](/wiki/Pentaho "Pentaho") Pentaho Open Source Business Intelligence Project has recently[*[when?](/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] added "Pentaho Metadata" which supports CWM

**Business Objects** (BO, BOBJ, or BObjects) was an [enterprise software](/wiki/Enterprise_software "Enterprise software") company, specializing in [business intelligence](/wiki/Business_intelligence "Business intelligence") (BI). Business Objects was acquired in 2007 by German company [SAP](/wiki/SAP "SAP"). The company claimed more than 46,000 customers in its final earnings release prior to being acquired by SAP.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Its flagship product was BusinessObjects XI (or BOXI[[2]](#cite_note-2)), with components that provide [performance management](/wiki/Performance_management "Performance management"), [planning](/wiki/Planning "Planning"), reporting, query and analysis, as well as [enterprise information management](/wiki/Enterprise_information_management "Enterprise information management"). Business Objects also offered consulting and education services to help customers deploy its business intelligence projects. Other toolsets enabled universes (the Business Objects name for a [semantic layer](/wiki/Semantic_layer "Semantic layer") between the physical data store and the front-end reporting tool) and ready-written reports to be stored centrally and made selectively available to communities of the users.

title: BusinessObjects
text:
## History

[Bernard Liautaud](/wiki/Bernard_Liautaud "Bernard Liautaud") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Liautaud "fr:Bernard Liautaud")] co-founded Business Objects in 1990 together with [Denis Payre](/wiki/Denis_Payre "Denis Payre") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Payre "fr:Denis Payre")], and was chief executive until September 2005, when he became chairman and chief executive until January 2008.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The concept of Business Objects and its initial implementation came from Jean-Michel Cambot.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1990, the first customer, [Coface](/wiki/Compagnie_Fran%C3%A7aise_d%27Assurance_pour_le_Commerce_Ext%C3%A9rieur "Compagnie Française d'Assurance pour le Commerce Extérieur"), was signed. The company went public on [NASDAQ](/wiki/NASDAQ "NASDAQ") in September 1994, making it the first European software company listed in the United States.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] In 2002, the company made *[Time](/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* magazine Europe's Digital Top 25 of 2002 and were *[BusinessWeek](/wiki/BusinessWeek "BusinessWeek")* Europe Stars of Europe.

On 7 October 2007, [SAP](/wiki/SAP "SAP") announced[[3]](#cite_note-3) that it would acquire Business Objects for $6.8 billion. As of 22 January 2008, the corporation was fully operated by SAP; this was seen as part of a growing consolidation trend in the business software industry, with [Oracle](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation") acquiring [Hyperion](/wiki/Hyperion_Solutions_Corporation "Hyperion Solutions Corporation") in 2007 and [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM") acquiring [Cognos](/wiki/Cognos "Cognos") in 2008.

title: BusinessObjects
text:
### Legal

On April 2, 2007, a lawsuit from [Informatica](/wiki/Informatica "Informatica") (inherited by Business Objects from the purchase of Acta Technologies in 2002) resulted in an award of $25 million in damages to Informatica for [patent infringement](/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement"). The lawsuit related to embedded data flows with one input and one output. Informatica asserted that the ActaWorks product (later sold by Business Objects as part of [Data Integrator](/wiki/BusinessObjects_Data_Integrator "BusinessObjects Data Integrator")), infringed several Informatica patents including US Patent Nos. 6,014,670 and 6,339,775, both titled "Apparatus and Method for Performing Data Transformations in Data Warehousing." Business Objects subsequently released a new version of [Data Integrator](/wiki/BusinessObjects_Data_Integrator "BusinessObjects Data Integrator") (11.7.2) which removed the infringing product capability.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

title: BusinessObjects
text:
### Timeline

- 1990: Business Objects launches Skipper SQL 2.0.x.
- 1994: Launches BusinessObjects v3.0 and goes public on the NASDAQ in September — the first French software company listed in the United States.[[5]](#cite_note-5)
- 1996: Enters the OLAP market and launches BusinessObjects v4.0. Bernard Liautaud named one of BusinessWeek's "Hottest Entrepreneurs of the Year."
- 1997: Introduces WebIntelligence thin client, which enables shared information across an extranet.[[6]](#cite_note-BOref-6)
- 1999: [General Electric](/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") (GE) begins working with the company.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Business Objects goes public in France on the Premier Marché. Acquires Next Action Technologies.
- 2000: Acquires OLAP@Work for approximately $15 million[[7]](#cite_note-7) and announces MDX Connect from this acquisition.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
- 2001: SAP signs an OEM and reseller agreement to bundle Crystal Reports. Acquires Blue Edge Software.
- 2001: Signs up its single largest global software licensing transaction with Three, formerly known as Hutchison 3G.
- 2002: Acquires Acta Technologies.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Bernard Liautaud named to Business Week's "Stars of Europe," and the company is named one of the "100 Fastest Growing Tech Companies" by Business 2.0.[[10]](#cite_note-10) [Informatica](/wiki/Informatica "Informatica") files a lawsuit against Acta, claiming patent rights infringement.[[6]](#cite_note-BOref-6)
- 2003: Acquires [Crystal Decisions](/wiki/Crystal_Decisions "Crystal Decisions") for $820 million.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Business Objects releases Dashboard Manager, BusinessObjects Enterprise 6, and BusinessObjects Performance Manager.

title: BusinessObjects
text:
- 2004: Debuts new combined company with the slogan, "Our Future is Clear, Crystal Clear." Launches Crystal v10 and BusinessObjects v6.5.
- 2005: Launches BusinessObjects XI. Acquires SRC Software, Infommersion, and Medience. Launches BusinessObjects Enterprise XI Release 2.
- 2006: Business Objects acquires Firstlogic, Inc and [Nsite Software, Inc.](/wiki/Nsite_Software_(Platform_as_a_Service) "Nsite Software (Platform as a Service)")[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)
- 2006: Acquires ALG Software (formerly Armstrong Laing Group).[[14]](#cite_note-14) Launches Crystal Xcelsius, which allows users to transform Microsoft Excel spreadsheet data into interactive Flash media files.
- 2007: Continuing its string of acquisitions, Business Objects acquires Cartesis[[15]](#cite_note-15) and [Inxight](/wiki/Inxight "Inxight").
- 2007: In October, [SAP](/wiki/SAP "SAP")'s Chief Executive [Henning Kagermann](/wiki/Henning_Kagermann "Henning Kagermann") announced a $6.8 billion deal to acquire Business Objects.[[16]](#cite_note-16)
- 2008: In January, SAP absorbs all of Business Objects' offices, and renames the entity "Business Objects, an SAP company". Following the acquisition of Business Objects by SAP, the founder and CEO of Business Objects, Bernard Liautaud, announces his resignation.[[17]](#cite_note-17)
- 2009: Business Objects becomes a division of SAP instead of a separate company. The portfolio brand "SAP BusinessObjects" was created. Some former Business Objects employees now officially work for SAP.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

title: Apatar
text:
## History

Apatar open source project was founded in 2005.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The first version of the tool was released under the GPLv2 license at www.sourceforge.net in February 2007. In April 2007, Apatar alpha version was demonstrated to its strategic partners, including [MySQL](/wiki/MySQL "MySQL") and BlackDuck. Apatar, Inc.,[[2]](#cite_note-2) a commercial company that provides support for the Apatar open source software, was founded in 2007 [[3]](#cite_note-3) as a branch of [Altoros](/wiki/Altoros "Altoros").

title: Apatar
text:
## Products

The company’s main product is **Apatar**,[[4]](#cite_note-mashup-4)[[5]](#cite_note-apatar_explained-5) a cross-platform open source desktop data integration tool that provides connectivity to a variety of databases, applications, protocols, files, and many more.

Donnelley](/wiki/RR_Donnelley "RR Donnelley"), [Autodesk](/wiki/Autodesk "Autodesk").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) and more.

title: Dataupia
text:
## History

Dataupia was founded in 2005 by Foster D. Hinshaw for analytics in "[big data](/wiki/Big_data "Big data")" applications such as for telecom and auto-reporting for the [Internet of things](/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things").

A classic definition of the [data warehouse](/wiki/Data_warehouse "Data warehouse") focuses on data storage.[[1]](#cite_note-InmonDefinition-1) However, the means to retrieve and analyze data, to [extract, transform and load](/wiki/Extract,_transform_and_load "Extract, transform and load") data, and to manage the dictionary data are also considered essential components of a [data warehouse appliance](/wiki/Data_warehouse_appliance "Data warehouse appliance") system. The Dataupia Satori Server provided all aspects of the [data warehouse appliance](/wiki/Data_warehouse_appliance "Data warehouse appliance") in a single product.

The company has headquarters in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), with additional offices in Binghamton, United Kingdom. The company was privately held.[[2]](#cite_note-DataupiaFactSheet-2)

Dataupia's name is a [portmanteau](/wiki/Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of the words "data", in reference to the data warehousing industry, and "[utopia](/wiki/Utopia "Utopia")". The combination of words is used by the company to imply ideal access to data.

title: Dataupia
text:
Dataupia's name is a [portmanteau](/wiki/Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of the words "data", in reference to the data warehousing industry, and "[utopia](/wiki/Utopia "Utopia")". The combination of words is used by the company to imply ideal access to data.

The Dataupia flagship product, Satori Server, is a network-attached [data warehouse appliance](/wiki/Data_warehouse_appliance "Data warehouse appliance") announced in 2007.[[3]](#cite_note-ProductReview1-3) As an appliance, it includes an embedded copy of Linux, a database engine, an aggregation engine, built-in storage, and parallel processors. In contrast to other custom-assembly data warehouse appliances, the Satori Server worked with existing database management systems, rather than requiring them to be replaced. In theory, this would appeal to customers with a huge investment in databases and data warehouse and [business intelligence](/wiki/Business_intelligence "Business intelligence") applications.[[4]](#cite_note-DataupiaLaunch-4)[[5]](#cite_note-SatoriServer-5)
Competitors included [Teradata](/wiki/Teradata "Teradata") and [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM") (which acquired [Netezza](/wiki/Netezza "Netezza") in 2010).[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In January 2009 Hinshaw temporarily left due to health problems, and Tony Sirianni became chief executive through November.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
During the [Great Recession](/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), the company reduced its staff and by August 2009 was seeking a buyer for its assets.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
By 2017, the company had not issued a press release since the 4.0 version of the product was announced in February 2011.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## History

Aster Data was co-founded in 2005 by [Stanford University](/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") graduate students George Candea, Mayank Bawa, and Tasso Argyros.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-close-2) It received funding from [First Round Capital](/wiki/First_Round_Capital "First Round Capital"), [Sequoia Capital](/wiki/Sequoia_Capital "Sequoia Capital"), [Institutional Venture Partners](/wiki/Institutional_Venture_Partners "Institutional Venture Partners"), Cambrian Ventures, [Jafco Ventures](/wiki/Jafco_Ventures "Jafco Ventures") as well as [angel investors](/wiki/Angel_investor "Angel investor"), including [Rajeev Motwani](/wiki/Rajeev_Motwani "Rajeev Motwani"), [Ron Conway](/wiki/Ron_Conway "Ron Conway") and [David Cheriton](/wiki/David_Cheriton "David Cheriton").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
It received its first round of funding of $5 million in 2005, a second round of $17 million in February 2009, and third round of $30 million in September 2010.[[4]](#cite_note-crunch-4)

Aster was mentioned in 2010 by [Intelligent Enterprise](/wiki/Intelligent_Enterprise_(magazine) "Intelligent Enterprise (magazine)")' editor.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)
It was ranked seventh in 2011 of venture-funded companies by *[The Wall Street Journal](/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")*.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
Argyros (Chief Technical Officer at the time) was listed as a technology pioneer of information technology and new media by the [World Economic Forum](/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum") in 2011.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

**Exasol** is an analytics engine, an in-memory database company headquartered in Germany, EU. It supports a wide range of use cases, from standalone data warehouse deployments to analytics acceleration and AI/ML model enablement. Its technology is based on [in-memory](/wiki/In_memory_database "In memory database"), [column-oriented](/wiki/Column-oriented_DBMS "Column-oriented DBMS"), [relational database management systems](/wiki/Relational_database_management_systems "Relational database management systems").[[1]](#cite_note-DBMS2-1)

Since 2008, Exasol led the [Transaction Processing Performance Council](/wiki/Transaction_Processing_Performance_Council "Transaction Processing Performance Council")'s TPC-H benchmark for analytical scenarios, in all data volume-based categories 100 GB, 300 GB, 1 TB, 3 TB, 10 TB, 30 TB and 100 TB.[[2]](#cite_note-TPC-H_Website-2) Exasol holds the top position in absolute performance as well as price/performance.

title: Exasol
text:
## Products

Exasol is a parallelized [relational database management system](/wiki/Relational_database_management_system "Relational database management system") (RDBMS) which runs on a cluster of standard computer hardware servers. Following the [SPMD](/wiki/SPMD "SPMD") model, on each node the identical code is executed simultaneously. The data is stored in a column-oriented way and proprietary in-memory compression methods are used. The company claims that tuning efforts are not necessary since the database includes some kind of automatic self-optimization (like automatic indices, table statistics, and distributing of data).[[1]](#cite_note-DBMS2-1)

Exasol is designed to run [in memory](/wiki/In-memory_database "In-memory database"), although data is persistently stored on disk following the [ACID](/wiki/ACID "ACID") rules. Exasol supports the [SQL Standard 2003](/wiki/SQL:2003 "SQL:2003") via interfaces like [ODBC](/wiki/Open_Database_Connectivity "Open Database Connectivity"), [JDBC](/wiki/Java_Database_Connectivity "Java Database Connectivity") or [ADO.NET](/wiki/ADO.NET "ADO.NET"). A [software development kit](/wiki/Software_development_kit "Software development kit") (SDK) is provided for native integration.[[3]](#cite_note-InDetail-3) For [online analytical processing](/wiki/Online_analytical_processing "Online analytical processing") (OLAP) applications, the [Multidimensional Expressions](/wiki/Multidimensional_Expressions "Multidimensional Expressions") (MDX) extension of SQL is supported via [OLE DB for OLAP](/wiki/OLE_DB_for_OLAP "OLE DB for OLAP") and [XML for Analysis](/wiki/XML_for_Analysis "XML for Analysis").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The license model is based on the allocated RAM for the database software (per GB RAM) and independent to the physical hardware. Customers gain the maximal performance if their compressed active data fits into that licensed RAM, but it can also be much larger.

Exasol has implemented a so-called cluster operating system (**EXACluster OS**). It is based on [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") and provides a runtime environment and storage layer for the RDBMS, employing a proprietary, cluster-based file system (ExaStorage). Cluster management algorithms are provided like failover mechanisms or automatic cluster installation.[[1]](#cite_note-DBMS2-1)[[3]](#cite_note-InDetail-3)

**BioMart** is a community-driven project to provide a single point of access to distributed [research data](/wiki/Research_data "Research data"). The BioMart project contributes [open source software](/wiki/Open_source_software "Open source software") and data services to the international [scientific community](/wiki/Scientific_community "Scientific community"). Although the BioMart software is primarily used by the [biomedical research](/wiki/Biomedical_research "Biomedical research") community, it is designed in such a way that any type of data can be incorporated into the BioMart framework. The BioMart project originated at the [European Bioinformatics Institute](/wiki/European_Bioinformatics_Institute "European Bioinformatics Institute") as a data management solution[[1]](#cite_note-pmid14707178-1) for the [Human Genome Project](/wiki/Human_Genome_Project "Human Genome Project").[[2]](#cite_note-pmid11237011-2) Since then, BioMart has grown to become a multi-institute collaboration involving various database projects on five continents.[[3]](#cite_note-pmid19144180-3)[[4]](#cite_note-pmid22083790-4)[[5]](#cite_note-pmid19420058-5)[[6]](#cite_note-pmid21930507-6)

title: BioMart
text:
## Integration with Ensembl

BioMart is a powerful tool for researchers and bioinformaticians that allows a user to export data from Ensembl, this could include data such as gene ID's, gene positions, associated variations, protein domains and sequences. BioMArt allows the data to be exported into convenient file types like FASTA, XLS, CSV, TSV, HTML. Researchers can use the exported data in a variety of applications, including genomic studies, gene expression analysis, and comparative genomics. BioMart's intuitive interface enables users to customize queries to access specific data sets or features of interest easily[[7]](#cite_note-7)

title: BioMart
text:
## Software

BioMart is a freely available, [open-source](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software"), [federated database system](/wiki/Federated_database_system "Federated database system") that provides unified access to disparate, geographically distributed data sources.[[8]](#cite_note-pmid21930506-8) BioMart allows databases hosted on different [servers](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)") to be presented seamlessly to users, facilitating collaborative projects. BioMart contains several levels of [query optimization](/wiki/Query_optimization "Query optimization") to efficiently manage large data sets, and offers a diverse selection of [graphical user interfaces](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") and [application programming interfaces](/wiki/Application_programming_interface "Application programming interface") to allow queries to be performed in whatever manner is most convenient for the user. BioMart's capabilities are extended by integration with several widely used software packages such as [Bioconductor](/wiki/Bioconductor "Bioconductor"),[[9]](#cite_note-pmid16082012-9) [Galaxy](/wiki/Galaxy_(computational_biology) "Galaxy (computational biology)"),[[10]](#cite_note-pmid24462600-10) [Cytoscape](/wiki/Cytoscape "Cytoscape"),[[11]](#cite_note-pmid20656902-11) and [Taverna](/wiki/Apache_Taverna "Apache Taverna").[[12]](#cite_note-pmid23640334-12)

title: BioMart
text:
## Data sources and community

There are around 40 BioMart data sources including the [Atlas of UTR Regulatory Activity](/wiki/Atlas_of_UTR_Regulatory_Activity "Atlas of UTR Regulatory Activity") (AURA), the [COSMIC cancer database](/wiki/COSMIC_cancer_database "COSMIC cancer database"), [Ensembl](/wiki/Ensembl "Ensembl") Genomes, [HapMap](/wiki/International_HapMap_Project "International HapMap Project"), [InterPro](/wiki/InterPro "InterPro"), [Mouse Genome Informatics](/wiki/Mouse_Genome_Informatics "Mouse Genome Informatics") (MGI), [Rfam](/wiki/Rfam "Rfam") and [UniProt](/wiki/UniProt "UniProt"). Access is provided by institutions including the [European Bioinformatics Institute](/wiki/European_Bioinformatics_Institute "European Bioinformatics Institute") (EBI) and the [Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute](/wiki/Wellcome_Trust_Sanger_Institute "Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute") in the UK, [Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory](/wiki/Cold_Spring_Harbor_Laboratory "Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory") and the [National Center for Biotechnology Information](/wiki/National_Center_for_Biotechnology_Information "National Center for Biotechnology Information") (NCBI) in the United States and [French National Centre for Scientific Research](/wiki/Centre_national_de_la_recherche_scientifique "Centre national de la recherche scientifique") (CNRS).[[13]](#cite_note-community-13) The BioMart Central Portal was established to provide a convenient single point of access to this growing pool of data sources.[[3]](#cite_note-pmid19144180-3)[[5]](#cite_note-pmid19420058-5)[[6]](#cite_note-pmid21930507-6)

**Amazon Redshift** is a [data warehouse](/wiki/Data_warehouse "Data warehouse") product which forms part of the larger [cloud-computing](/wiki/Cloud-computing "Cloud-computing") platform [Amazon Web Services](/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services "Amazon Web Services").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It is built on top of technology from the [massive parallel processing](/wiki/Massive_parallel_processing "Massive parallel processing") (MPP) data warehouse company [ParAccel](/wiki/ParAccel "ParAccel") (later acquired by [Actian](/wiki/Actian "Actian")),[[2]](#cite_note-2) to handle large scale [data sets](/wiki/Data_set "Data set") and [database migrations](/wiki/Database#Migration "Database"). Redshift differs from Amazon's other hosted database offering, [Amazon RDS](/wiki/Amazon_RDS "Amazon RDS"), in its ability to handle analytic workloads on [big data](/wiki/Big_data "Big data") data sets stored by a [column-oriented DBMS](/wiki/Column-oriented_DBMS "Column-oriented DBMS") principle. Redshift allows up to 16 [petabytes](/wiki/Petabyte "Petabyte") of data on a cluster.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Redshift uses parallel processing and [compression](/wiki/Data_compression "Data compression") to decrease command [execution time](/wiki/Runtime_(program_lifecycle_phase) "Runtime (program lifecycle phase)").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

**Fluentd** is a [cross-platform](/wiki/Cross_platform "Cross platform") [open-source](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") [data collection](/wiki/Data_collection "Data collection") software project originally developed at [Treasure Data](/wiki/Treasure_Data "Treasure Data"). It is written primarily in the [C](/wiki/C_(Programming_Language) "C (Programming Language)") programming language with a thin-[Ruby](/wiki/Ruby_(programming_language) "Ruby (programming language)") wrapper that gives users flexibility.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: Fluentd
text:
## Overview

Fluentd was positioned for "[big data](/wiki/Big_data "Big data")," semi- or un-structured data sets. It analyzes [event logs](/wiki/Logfile#Event_logs "Logfile"), [application](/wiki/Application_software "Application software") logs, and [clickstreams](/wiki/Clickstream "Clickstream").[[3]](#cite_note-3) According to Suonsyrjä and Mikkonen, the "core idea of Fluentd is to be the unifying layer between different types of log inputs and outputs.",[[4]](#cite_note-4) Fluentd is available on [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux"), [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS"), and [Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Fluentd was created by Sadayuki Furuhashi as a project of the [Mountain View](/wiki/Mountain_View,_California "Mountain View, California")-based firm Treasure Data. Written primarily in [Ruby](/wiki/Ruby_(programming_language) "Ruby (programming language)"), its source code was released as [open-source software](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") in October 2011.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-fluentd-architecture-7) The company announced $5 million of funding in 2013.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
Treasure Data was then sold to [Arm Ltd.](/wiki/Arm_Ltd. "Arm Ltd.") in 2018.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

title: Fluentd
text:
## Users

Fluentd was one of the data collection tools recommended by [Amazon Web Services](/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services "Amazon Web Services") in 2013, when it was said to be similar to [Apache Flume](/wiki/Apache_Flume "Apache Flume") or [Scribe](/wiki/Scribe_(log_server) "Scribe (log server)").[[10]](#cite_note-10) [Google Cloud Platform](/wiki/Google_Cloud_Platform "Google Cloud Platform")'s [BigQuery](/wiki/BigQuery "BigQuery") recommends Fluentd as the default real-time data-ingestion tool, and uses Google's customized version of Fluentd, called google-fluentd, as a default logging agent.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

## Fluent Bit

Fluent Bit is a log processor and log forwarder that is being developed as a [CNCF](/wiki/Cloud_Native_Computing_Foundation "Cloud Native Computing Foundation") sub-project under the umbrella of Fluent project.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Fluentd is written in [C](/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)") and [Ruby](/wiki/Ruby_(programming_language) "Ruby (programming language)") and consumes at least 60 [megabytes](/wiki/Megabyte "Megabyte") of memory. [Fluent Bit](/wiki/Fluent_Bit "Fluent Bit") is written only in C, with no dependencies, and consumes approximately one megabyte of memory, making it easier to run under [embedded Linux](/wiki/Linux_on_embedded_systems "Linux on embedded systems") and in [containers](/wiki/Containerization_(computing) "Containerization (computing)").[[14]](#cite_note-14)

## History

ClickHouse’s technology was first developed at [Yandex](/wiki/Yandex "Yandex"), Russia's largest technology company.[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2009, Alexey Milovidov and developers started an experimental project to check the hypothesis if it was viable to generate analytical reports in real-time from non-[aggregated data](/wiki/Aggregate_data "Aggregate data") that is also constantly added in real-time. The developers spent 3 years to prove this hypothesis, and in 2012 ClickHouse launched in production for the first time to power [Yandex.Metrica](/wiki/Yandex.Metrica "Yandex.Metrica").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Since ClickHouse became available as open source in 2016, its popularity has grown, as evidenced through adoption by industry-leading companies like [Uber](/wiki/Uber "Uber"), [Comcast](/wiki/Comcast "Comcast"), [eBay](/wiki/EBay "EBay"), and [Cisco](/wiki/Cisco "Cisco").[[6]](#cite_note-6) ClickHouse was also implemented at [CERN's](/wiki/CERN "CERN") [LHCb experiment](/wiki/LHCb_experiment "LHCb experiment") to store and process [metadata](/wiki/Metadata "Metadata") on 10 billion events with over 1000 attributes per event.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: ClickHouse
text:
### Acquisitions

ClickHouse, Inc. has made the following acquisitions:

- **Arctype** — October 2022. Arctype's SQL client was integrated into ClickHouse Cloud to provide a web-based interface that formed the basis for the Cloud Console.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
- **chDB** — March 2024. chDB is an in-process OLAP SQL engine that embeds the ClickHouse engine as a [library](/wiki/Software_library "Software library"), allowing analytical queries to run inside a host application rather than against a separate server.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
- **PeerDB** — July 2024. PeerDB provides change data capture (CDC) technology that enables replication from [PostgreSQL](/wiki/PostgreSQL "PostgreSQL") into ClickHouse, expanding real-time analytics capabilities. ClickHouse, Inc. offers a hosted version of PeerDB through ClickPipes, a managed ingestion service for ClickHouse Cloud that supports seamless integration with Postgres sources.[[9]](#cite_note-9)
- **HyperDX** — March 2025. HyperDX is an open-source observability platform built on ClickHouse, providing a user interface and observability tooling that were integrated into ClickHouse's observability stack. HyperDX now serves as the primary UI for ClickStack, an open-source observability stack based on ClickHouse.[[10]](#cite_note-10)
- **LibreChat** — November 2025. LibreChat is an open-source platform that provides a unified chat interface for interacting with large language models. It became part of ClickHouse's open-source "Agentic Data Stack".[[11]](#cite_note-11)
- **Langfuse** — January 2026. Langfuse is an open-source platform for large language model observability, evaluation, and prompt management. The acquisition was announced alongside a US$400 million Series D funding round.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)

## History

It started at [RJMetrics](/wiki/RJMetrics "RJMetrics") in 2016 as a solution to add basic transformation capabilities to Stitch (acquired by Talend in 2018).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The earliest versions of dbt allowed analysts to contribute to the data transformation process following the best practices of software engineering.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

From the beginning, dbt was open source.[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2018, the dbt Labs team (then called Fishtown Analytics) released a commercial product on top of dbt Core.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In January 2025, dbt Labs acquired SDF Labs, a Seattle-based startup developing SQL compilation and static analysis technology for analytics engineering.[[7]](#cite_note-7) SDF Labs was founded in 2022 by Lukas Schulte, Wolfram Schulte, Elias DeFaria, and Michael Levin.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Funding

In April 2020, dbt Labs announced its Series A led by [Andreessen Horowitz](/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz").[[9]](#cite_note-9) In November, dbt Labs announced its Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and [Sequoia](/wiki/Sequoia_Capital "Sequoia Capital").[[10]](#cite_note-10) And in June 2021, dbt Labs raised its Series C led by [Altimeter](/wiki/Altimeter_Capital "Altimeter Capital"), Sequoia, and Andreessen Horowitz.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In February 2022, the company raised $222 million for its Series D, at a $4.2 billion valuation.[[12]](#cite_note-12) In October 2025, dbt Labs announced a definitive agreement to merge with Fivetran in an all-stock deal, with Fivetran CEO George Fraser to lead the combined company and dbt Labs founder Tristan Handy serving as president; the merger was pending regulatory approval as of 2026, with the combined entity projected to approach $600 million in annual recurring revenue.[[13]](#cite_note-fivetran-dbt-merger-13)

title: Data build tool
text:
## Overview

Dbt enables analytics engineers to transform data in their warehouses by writing select statements, and turns these select statements into tables and views. Dbt does the transformation (T) in [extract, load, transform](/wiki/Extract,_load,_transform "Extract, load, transform") (ELT) processes – it does not extract or load data, but is designed to be performant at transforming data already inside of a warehouse. Dbt has the goal of allowing analysts to work more like software engineers, in line with the dbt viewpoint.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Dbt uses [YAML](/wiki/YAML "YAML") files to declare properties. `seed` is a type of [reference table](/wiki/Reference_table "Reference table") used in dbt for static or infrequently changed data, like for example [country codes](/wiki/List_of_ISO_3166_country_codes "List of ISO 3166 country codes") or [lookup tables](/wiki/Lookup_table "Lookup table")), which are [CSV](/wiki/Comma_separated_values "Comma separated values") based and typically stored in a seeds [folder](/wiki/Directory_(computing) "Directory (computing)").

**DuckDB** is an [open-source](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") [column-oriented](/wiki/Column-oriented_DBMS "Column-oriented DBMS") [Relational Database Management System](/wiki/Relational_Database_Management_System "Relational Database Management System") (RDBMS).[[1]](#cite_note-1) It is designed to provide high performance on complex queries against large databases in embedded configuration,[[2]](#cite_note-Kamphuis_2020_pp._608–612-2) such as combining [tables](/wiki/Table_(database) "Table (database)") with hundreds of columns and billions of rows. Unlike other embedded databases (for example, [SQLite](/wiki/SQLite "SQLite")) DuckDB is not focusing on transactional ([OLTP](/wiki/OLTP "OLTP")) applications and instead is specialized for [online analytical processing](/wiki/Online_analytical_processing "Online analytical processing") (OLAP) workloads.[[3]](#cite_note-Raasveldt_Mühleisen_2019_pp._1981–1984-3) The project has over 6 million downloads per month.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-theregister.com-6)

## History

DuckDB was originally developed by [Mark Raasveldt](/w/index.php?title=Mark_Raasveldt&action=edit&redlink=1 "Mark Raasveldt (page does not exist)") and [Hannes Mühleisen](/w/index.php?title=Hannes_M%C3%BChleisen&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hannes Mühleisen (page does not exist)") [[wd](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q111338024#sitelinks-wikipedia "d:Special:EntityPage/Q111338024")] at the [Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica](/wiki/Centrum_Wiskunde_%26_Informatica "Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica") (CWI) in the [Netherlands](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands").[[2]](#cite_note-Kamphuis_2020_pp._608–612-2) The project co-founders designed DuckDB to address the need for an in-process OLAP database solution.[[7]](#cite_note-7) DuckDB was first released in 2019.[[8]](#cite_note-Clark-8) DuckDB version 1.0.0 was released on June 3, 2024, under the codename SnowDuck.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

title: DuckDB
text:
## Features

DuckDB uses a [vectorized query processing](/wiki/Vectorwise "Vectorwise") engine.[[3]](#cite_note-Raasveldt_Mühleisen_2019_pp._1981–1984-3) DuckDB is special amongst database management systems because it does not have any external dependencies and can be built with just a C++17 compiler.[[10]](#cite_note-10) DuckDB also deviates from the traditional [client–server model](/wiki/Client%E2%80%93server_model "Client–server model") by running inside a host process (it has bindings, for example, for a Python interpreter with the ability to directly place data into [NumPy](/wiki/NumPy "NumPy") arrays[[2]](#cite_note-Kamphuis_2020_pp._608–612-2)). DuckDB's SQL parser is derived from the pg_query library developed by Lukas Fittl, which is itself derived from [PostgreSQL](/wiki/PostgreSQL "PostgreSQL")'s SQL parser that has been stripped down as much as possible.[[3]](#cite_note-Raasveldt_Mühleisen_2019_pp._1981–1984-3)[[11]](#cite_note-11) DuckDB uses a single-file storage format to store data on
disk, designed to support efficient scans
and bulk updates, appends and deletes.[[12]](#cite_note-12) DuckDB is also compiled to [WebAssembly](/wiki/WebAssembly "WebAssembly") using [emscripten](/wiki/Emscripten "Emscripten") which enables DuckDB to run SQL in browser-based analytics tools.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

title: DuckDB
text:
## Comparison

DuckDB in its OLAP niche does not compete with the traditional DBMS like [MSSQL](/wiki/MSSQL "MSSQL"), [PostgreSQL](/wiki/PostgreSQL "PostgreSQL") and [Oracle database](/wiki/Oracle_database "Oracle database"). While using [SQL](/wiki/SQL "SQL") for queries, DuckDB targets serverless applications and provides extremely fast responses using either [Apache Parquet](/wiki/Apache_Parquet "Apache Parquet") files or its own format for storage. These attributes make it a popular choice for large dataset analysis in interactive mode.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

title: DuckDB
text:
## Commercial use

DuckDB is used at [Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook"), [Google](/wiki/Google "Google"), and [Airbnb](/wiki/Airbnb "Airbnb").[[16]](#cite_note-16)

DuckDB co-author Mühleisen also runs a support and consultancy firm for the software, DuckLabs.[[8]](#cite_note-Clark-8) The company has chosen not to take venture capital funding, stating "We feel investment would force the project direction towards monetization, and we would much prefer keeping DuckDB open and available for as many people as possible".[[6]](#cite_note-theregister.com-6) Another company, [MotherDuck](/wiki/MotherDuck "MotherDuck"), has received $100 million funding for its data platform based on DuckDB, with investors including [Andreessen Horowitz](/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz").[[17]](#cite_note-17)

The company DuckLabs was formerly known as DuckDB Labs.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

## DuckDB Foundation

The independent non-profit DuckDB Foundation safeguards the long-term maintenance and development of DuckDB. The foundation holds much of the intellectual property of the project and is funded by charitable donations.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The DuckDB Foundation's statutes ensure DuckDB remains open-source under the [MIT license](/wiki/MIT_License "MIT License") in perpetuity.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

## Extensions

DuckDB's architecture supports extensions, allowing additional functionality to be added dynamically.[[34]](#cite_note-34) Many popular extensions are maintained by the core DuckDB team, and there are over 30 community extensions maintained by third parties.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)

DuckDB's architecture supports dynamically loaded extensions. Core extensions maintained by the DuckDB team include:

- **httpfs** — remote file access via HTTP, HTTPS, and S3-compatible object storage (including Azure write support since v1.5)
- **spatial** — geospatial functions (ST_* family); GEOMETRY became a built-in core type in v1.5
- **iceberg** — Apache Iceberg table read/write, including REST catalog support
- **delta** — Delta Lake table read/write via the Delta Kernel
- **ducklake** — lakehouse format storing all metadata in a SQL database with ACID semantics; supports time travel, schema evolution, and multi-table transactions

There are also over 30 community extensions maintained by third parties, covering use cases from graph queries (SQL/PGQ) to Kafka integration and ML inference. A full list is available at the [DuckDB Community Extensions registry](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/list_of_extensions).
